title: Why do cats act so weird?
speaker: Tony Buffington (lesson); narrated by Addison Anderson
intro: Why do cats scratch the sofa, hide in boxes and want lots of small meals? A vet explains how their wild past shapes their behaviour today.
summary: Cats are hugely popular online, and the vet Tony Buffington explains their strange habits through evolution. Their wild ancestors were solitary hunters of small animals, but they were also prey for larger carnivores, and both roles shaped instincts that pet cats still have. Because their prey was small, wild cats had to stalk, pounce, kill and eat many times a day, which is why house cats like chasing toys and prefer several small meals spread over the day and night. Scratching keeps their claws in good condition, stretches their back and leg muscles and relieves stress, so it does not mean a cat hates your furniture. Cats like high perches because they can watch their surroundings, and they hide in boxes, bags and other small spaces because of their wild past. They want a clean litter box because, in the wild, smells could give away their location to predators. Purring is one behaviour that science still cannot fully explain.

vocab.m: an animal that hunts and eats other animals
an animal that is hunted and eaten by another animal
to follow an animal slowly and quietly in order to catch it
to jump suddenly onto something to catch it
a natural way of behaving that an animal is born with, not one it learns
a high place where an animal sits and watches

adv.title: Use three adverbs

levels.title: Less stuff, more happiness
levels.speaker: Graham Hill
levels.intro: Writer and designer Graham Hill lives in a very small flat. He asks: could less stuff and less space make us happier?
levels.summary: Graham Hill asks whether having less stuff in less space could make us happier. He says Americans have about three times as much space as 50 years ago, but there is still a 22-billion-dollar personal storage industry, and people are in debt and no happier. He started a project called LifeEdited and ran an online competition to design his 420-square-foot flat in Manhattan; more than 300 people sent ideas. Choosing 420 square feet instead of 600 saved him about 200,000 dollars and also means lower bills and a smaller footprint. He gives three rules: edit ruthlessly (get rid of things you do not need and think before you buy), think small (design for how you use things most of the time, choose things that nest or stack, and digitise books, films and papers), and make things multifunctional (a moving wall, a bed in the wall, fold-down guest beds and a coffee table that grows to seat ten). He does not say everyone must live in 420 square feet, but he asks people to imagine a smaller home and ends by saying that less might be more.

levels.title: How to speak so that people want to listen
levels.speaker: Julian Treasure
levels.intro: Sound expert Julian Treasure names the seven 'deadly sins' of speaking, offers four foundations for being heard, and ends with a vocal warm-up you can try at home.
levels.summary: Julian Treasure calls the human voice the instrument we all play and perhaps the most powerful sound in the world, and asks why so many people feel they are not heard. He lists seven deadly sins of speaking: gossip, judging, negativity, complaining (which he jokes is a national sport in Britain), excuses, embroidery or exaggeration, and dogmatism, which means confusing facts with opinions. Against these he sets four foundations, HAIL: honesty, authenticity, integrity and love, explaining that by love he means wishing people well. He then opens a vocal toolbox: register (speaking from the chest gives weight and authority), timbre (people prefer rich, smooth, warm voices, which can be trained), prosody (a monotone, or ending every sentence like a question, is hard to listen to), pace and pauses (silence is powerful, so there is no need to fill it with 'um'), pitch and volume. He leads the audience through a warm-up: arms up and a sigh, 'ba ba' and a lip trill, 'la la' and a rolled 'r', and a siren from a high 'wee' to a low 'aw', which he says is the one to do if you only do one. He ends by imagining a world where people speak powerfully, listen consciously and design spaces for sound.

vocab.m: talking about other people, often unkindly, when they are not present
presenting your opinions as if they were unquestionable facts
here: adding exaggerated or invented details to make a story more impressive
the quality of being genuinely yourself rather than playing a role
the particular quality or 'colour' of a voice, apart from its pitch and volume
the rhythm, stress and melody of speech that carry extra meaning

questions.why: He presents the siren as the single most useful exercise.

listen.q: Name at least three of the 'deadly sins' and explain why they put listeners off.
listen.hint: Gossip, judging, negativity, complaining, excuses, exaggeration, dogmatism.
listen.model: Gossip is a problem because anyone who talks badly about absent people will soon talk about you. Complaining spreads misery like a virus, and dogmatism, which means presenting opinions as facts, makes listeners feel bombarded.

listen.q: What does HAIL stand for, and why does it matter?
listen.hint: Four foundations, one for each letter.
listen.model: HAIL stands for honesty, authenticity, integrity and love. These four foundations make people trust you, because you are truthful, you are yourself, you do what you say and you wish your listeners well.

listen.q: Describe two tools from his vocal toolbox and what they do.
listen.hint: Register, timbre, prosody, pace, pitch, volume.
listen.model: Register matters, because speaking from the chest gives your voice weight and authority. Pace is another tool: slowing down adds emphasis, and a pause can be powerful, so there is no need to fill every silence with um.

syn.title: Summarise with precise vocabulary
syn.prompt: Write a summary of the talk in 100–150 words. Replace every underlined word with a more precise or formal synonym.
syn.text: Treasure [argues] that many people feel [ignored] when they speak. He [lists] seven [habits] that push listeners away and [offers] a [simple] alternative called HAIL.
syn.model: Julian Treasure contends that many people feel unheard when they speak, and he begins by describing the human voice as the most powerful instrument we have. He identifies seven deadly sins of speaking: gossip, judging, negativity, complaining, excuses, exaggeration and dogmatism. Each of these tendencies makes listeners less willing to pay attention. He then proposes an uncomplicated alternative called HAIL, which stands for honesty, authenticity, integrity and love. In the second half of the talk, he presents a vocal toolbox that includes register, timbre, prosody, pace, pitch and volume, and he leads the audience through a brief warm-up. He concludes that if we spoke consciously and listened carefully, understanding would become the norm.

rep.title: Formal account in reported speech
rep.prompt: Write a formal account of Treasure's main points for a staff newsletter (110–150 words), in reported speech. Use at least three different reporting verbs and no contractions.
rep.model: Julian Treasure began by stating that the human voice was the most powerful sound in the world. He acknowledged that many people felt that nobody listened to them and argued that seven common habits were partly responsible, including gossip, complaining and dogmatism. He remarked that complaining had become a national sport in Britain. He then proposed four foundations for powerful speech, namely honesty, authenticity, integrity and love, and stressed that love, in his sense, meant wishing people well. Turning to the voice itself, he explained that speaking from the chest gave a speaker more authority and that pauses could be extremely powerful. Finally, he recommended that everyone should warm up their voice before an important conversation, just as an athlete would warm up before a race.

arg.title: Argue a position
arg.prompt: 'How you say something matters more than what you say.' Write a formal argument (150–200 words). Use ideas from the talk, present the other side, and give your own view. No contractions.
starters: However, it could be argued that …
arg.model: It is often claimed that how we say something matters more than what we say. The talk by Julian Treasure certainly supports this view to some extent. He shows that register, pace and pitch can change the meaning of a simple question, and that a monotonous voice makes even good ideas difficult to follow. Moreover, listeners often decide whether to trust a speaker within seconds, long before they have analysed the arguments. However, it could be argued that delivery without substance is empty. A confident, warm voice cannot make a dishonest message honest, and Treasure himself places honesty and integrity at the foundation of good speaking. Furthermore, in written communication, which is a large part of modern life, tone of voice disappears entirely and only the content remains. In my view, the two cannot really be separated. Content gives a message its value, while delivery decides whether anyone receives it. Therefore, speakers should first make sure that they have something true and useful to say, and only then work on saying it well.

levels.title: How great leaders inspire action
levels.speaker: Simon Sinek
levels.intro: Simon Sinek draws a 'golden circle' on a flip chart and argues that the leaders and companies who inspire us all start with one question: why?
levels.summary: Simon Sinek asks why some people and organisations, such as Apple, Martin Luther King Jr. and the Wright brothers, achieve more than others with the same resources. His golden circle has three rings: what you do, how you do it and why you do it; everyone knows their what, some know their how, but very few can articulate their why, and profit is a result, not a purpose. Most organisations communicate from the outside in, starting with product features, while inspiring ones communicate from the inside out, as Apple does by starting from its belief in challenging the status quo; this, he says, is why Dell and Gateway failed when they sold MP3 players and flat-screen TVs. He links the circle to biology: the neocortex handles rational thought and language, while the limbic brain handles feelings such as trust and loyalty and drives decisions but has no capacity for language, which is why we talk of gut feelings. Samuel Pierpont Langley had 50,000 dollars from the War Department, the best minds and the press, yet the Wright brothers, funded by their bicycle shop, flew first on 17 December 1903, and Langley simply quit. Using the law of diffusion of innovation (innovators 2.5%, early adopters 13.5%, early majority 34%), he argues that mass success comes after about 15 to 18% of the market, and that TiVo failed because it sold features rather than a belief. About 250,000 people came to hear Martin Luther King in 1963 because they shared his beliefs; he gave the 'I have a dream' speech, not the 'I have a plan' speech. Sinek concludes that leaders hold authority, but those who lead inspire us, and we follow them because we want to.

syn.title: Summarise with sophisticated vocabulary
syn.prompt: Write a summary of the talk in 120–170 words. Replace every underlined word with a more precise or sophisticated synonym.
syn.text: Sinek [claims] that [successful] leaders [begin] with why. People buy why you do something, and this [belief] creates [loyal] customers and [committed] staff.
syn.model: Simon Sinek contends that the most influential leaders and organisations commence with why. He describes a golden circle of three rings, what, how and why, and observes that while every company knows what it does, very few can articulate why it exists. Profit, he insists, is a result rather than a purpose. Apple, in his account, communicates from the inside out, so customers buy into its conviction that the status quo should be challenged. He grounds this in biology: the limbic brain governs feelings and decisions but has no capacity for language, which is why we speak of gut feelings. The Wright brothers, funded only by a bicycle shop, defeated the lavishly resourced Samuel Pierpont Langley because their team shared a cause. Such shared conviction, Sinek maintains, produces devoted customers and wholehearted employees, and it explains why a quarter of a million people gathered to hear Martin Luther King.

rep.title: Formal account in reported speech
rep.prompt: Write a formal account of Sinek's argument for a management newsletter (130–170 words), in reported speech. Use at least three different reporting verbs and no contractions.
rep.model: In his talk, Simon Sinek contended that great leaders and organisations thought, acted and communicated in the same way, which was the opposite of everyone else. He observed that every company knew what it did, but he insisted that very few could explain why they did it. He argued that people did not buy what a company did but why it did it, and he illustrated this with Apple, which, he claimed, had persuaded customers to share its belief in challenging the status quo. He stated that the part of the brain responsible for decisions had no capacity for language, which was why people often said that a choice did not feel right. He also noted that the Wright brothers had succeeded where a much better funded rival had failed. He concluded that leaders held authority, whereas those who led inspired people to follow them willingly.

arg.title: Argue a position
arg.prompt: 'Customers buy what a company believes, not what it sells.' Write a formal argument (200–260 words). Use ideas from the talk, present the other side, and give your own view. No contractions.
starters: Nevertheless, critics would point out that …
arg.model: Simon Sinek famously argues that people do not buy what a company does but why it does it. It is undeniable that this idea captures something important about modern consumer behaviour. Brands such as Apple attract customers who identify with their values, and these customers often remain faithful even when competitors offer similar products at lower prices. Moreover, in crowded markets where products are increasingly alike, a clear sense of purpose may be one of the few genuine ways in which a company can distinguish itself. Nevertheless, critics would point out that this argument rests on carefully chosen success stories. For every company with an inspiring mission that thrives, there are others with equally noble statements that fail because their products are poor, their prices too high or their timing wrong. Furthermore, many everyday purchases, from petrol to washing powder, are driven largely by price and convenience, and few shoppers know or care what the manufacturer believes. Consequently, it would be naive to suggest that purpose alone can sustain a business. I would argue that belief and quality are complementary rather than competing. A compelling purpose can turn satisfied customers into devoted ones, but only if the product itself keeps its promise. In my opinion, the most enduring companies combine a credible why with a what that people actually need, so the insight is valuable as long as it is not mistaken for the whole story.
